83. Three Levels of Command in Japanese: 
て-form commands, なさい, な-commands, imperative form.
Three Levels of Command in Japanese: て-form commands, なさい, な-commands, imperative form. Lesson 83
こんにちは。
Today we're going to talk about
ways of making commands and requests in Japanese.
You'll probably know some of these already,
but I think we're going to go a little bit deeper
to some things you may not have realized.
We're going to go from the least commanding and intense towards the most,
so we'll start off with one that we all know, which is the て-form.
The て-form
Some sources will tell you that the て-form on its own is a command or request form.
That's only half true. It's the abbreviation of a command or request.
If we say "ちょっと待って" (wait a little), this is an abbreviation
of "ちょっと待ってください" (wait a little please)

【図】Two girls in blue uniforms and red backpacks with pink petals falling; the girl in front wears a yellow hat with a pink flower, and the girl behind waves. A speech bubble with its tail pointing to her reads 「ちょっと待って」. No diagram labels or arrows.

and probably because of this
it's the one that's least likely to be offensive, although it's still casual.
Now, sometimes you'll hear people saying not "ちょっと待って"
but "ちょっと待ってて". What's going on here?
【図】A large adult penguin bends toward a small grey chick, with two speech bubbles: the adult's ちょっと待ってて and the chick's はーい, each tail pointing to its speaker. No arrows.
Essentially what they're saying is "Wait a little bit and I'll be back".
The implication is that the waiting period will end fairly shortly.
And what this actually is is a contraction of "ちょっと待っていて".
As we know "待っている" means "exist in a state of waiting", "be waiting", in English.
So "ちょっと待ってて" is actually taking this "待っている" and putting it into て-form,
so that what you're being asked or instructed to do is exist in a state of waiting.
And the implication of this is, just exist for a little bit in a state of waiting.
And of course this doesn't have to be waiting, it can be anything,
but the implication is, just do it for a bit, just exist in that state for a short time.
If we don't say "ちょっと" (and we don't necessarily)
there's nothing to indicate a short time, but that is always the implication
of telling someone with the て-form to exist in a particular state.
て-form with ない helper adjective
The other thing to know about the て-form which is used to tell or ask someone
to do something is that, as we know, the equivalent negative adjective of any verb
is made by simply attaching the helper adjective "ない" to the あ-stem.
And the helper adjective "ない" actually is unusual in that it has two て-forms.
It has the regular て-form, which is formed just like any other て-form,
by attaching -て to the く-stem, so that's "なくて",
but it also has the irregular て-form "ないで".

【図】A large close-up panda on the left cries with blue teardrops on both sides and a frowning mouth, facing a smaller seated panda with shiny eyes and pink cheeks at right. A speech bubble at lower left reads 泣かないで (“Don’t cry”) and its tail points to the small panda; no diagram labels or arrows.
And when attached to a verb this is only used in two kinds of circumstance.
ないで - irregular て-form of ない
One is when we say "do B without doing A",
so "話さないで歩く" means "walk without talking".
The other is when we're making that て-formed command or request.
And again it's short for "ないでください".
So if we say "泣かないで" (don't cry),
that's using this secondary, specialized て-form of "ない",
which is specifically there for making negative commands or requests,
as well as for the one other usage that we discussed.
And sometimes in anime you'll hear someone scream,
when a monster is approaching her, "来ないで!" (don't come).

【図】Panicked light-brown-haired cartoon woman in a blue jacket, white shirt and dotted tie, with sweat lines and raised hands, under a red jagged speech bubble reading 来ないで！. No diagram labels or arrows.
In English we'd probably say "Keep away!" In Japanese we say "来ないで!"

【図】Dark-mode YouTube comment screenshot with like/dislike and Reply UI, not a diagram. The top comment asks whether なくて is the て-form of ない as an adjective while [verb] + ないで is the て-form of that negated verb; @organicjapanesewithcuredol49 replies “No,” arguing 食べない is not a “negated verb,” ない is always functionally an adjective, ないで is not invariably used when ない is a helper, and 食べなくてもいい uses the regular ないて-form. Japanese tokens as printed: なくて, ない, ないで, 食べない, 食べなくてもいい, ないて-form. No labels or arrows.
なさい
Now, next up in our hierarchy of commands is "なさい".
"なさい" is attached to the い-stem of verbs, and
when you attach "なさい" to the い-stem of a verb, you make it into a command.

【図】Hiragana chart: the い-column boxed green and the う-column boxed red, with green arrows pointing left from the u-column to the i-column. Green label +なさい sits at right, and the note reads "Ichidan ('ru-verb'): always just delete the る" — the rule for forming the なさい command.
So, "起きなさい" is "get up / wake up";
"落ち着きなさい" (calm down, settle down),
we're attaching "なさい" to the い-stem of "落ち着く",
which means "calm down" or "settle down" and turning it into a command.
"なさい" is the sort of command given by parents to children,
teachers to a class, that sort of thing.
It's not offensive if it's given by someone who's entitled to give it.
So, for example, in the anime "借りぐらしのアリエッティ",
Arietty's father says "寝なさい".
That's the い-stem, which of course with ichidan verbs we make by simply
removing the -る, of "寝る" (sleep, or go to bed) plus "なさい".
な - the abbreviation of なさい
Something that can be confusing here is that there is an abbreviation of "なさい"
which can be confused with a different abbreviation meaning the opposite.
And that abbreviation is "な".
When we attach "な" to the い-stem of a verb, then we're actually abbreviating "なさい".
So if we say "準備しな", we're saying "準備しなさい" (get ready, get prepared):
"準備する", い-stem of "する", "し" + "なさい" or "な".
【図】Anime-style girl with long purple hair, yellow hair clip and black blazer, arms crossed. Text reads 準備しな, a blunt imperative meaning "get ready". No labels or arrows.
Now, that in itself isn't particularly confusing.
What can confuse people is that if we say, for example,
"バカにするな" (don't make fun of me, of her);
【図】Angry pink cartoon rabbit head with long ears, slanted brows and a frown, with a large speech bubble whose tail points to it; the bubble reads バカにするな!. No other labels or arrows.
"それを食べるな" (don't eat that! [could be poison]).
This means the opposite!
We're using "な" for both a command to do something
and a command not to do something.
So how do we tell the two apart? Fortunately, it's very easy.
If the "な" is attached to the い-stem, then it's an abbreviation of "なさい".

【図】Hiragana chart あ い う え お / か き く け こ / さ し す せ そ / た ち つ て と / な に ぬ ね の / ば び ぶ べ ぼ / ま み む め も / ら り る れ ろ, with a red box around う く す つ ぬ ぶ む る and a green box around い き し ち に び み り. Green arrows point left from the red う column to the green い column; green text reads +な =なさい and the caption reads "Ichidan (\"ru-verb\"): always just delete the る."
It always is.
If it's not attached to the い-stem but attached to the entire logical clause
as in "それを食べるな", then it is not an abbreviation of "なさい".
It's in fact an older negative related to "ない".

【図】Two cartoon pandas: the upper holds a fish with mouth open, the lower scowls and scolds it. The speech bubble それを食べるな ("Don't eat that," negative imperative な) points to the lower panda; no arrows or labels.
So really, although they can seem confusing at first
and they're probably confusing when you're told by some textbook just
to learn which particular forms they stick to, it's not really confusing in practice.
One only attaches where "なさい" would attach to the い-stem,
and that's the one that means "なさい"!
The other one tops off a complete logical clause with the negativizing "な".
Note: Some further info Dolly gives about なさい in the comments

【図】A dark YouTube comment screenshot from @organicjapanesewithcuredol49 explaining that なさる is honorific and なさい after the い-stem is mostly a command form (命令形), with おやすみなさい and ごめんなさい (御免なさい) as set expressions. No diagram labels or arrows.
The real command / imperative form - 命令形
And now we come to the real command form, "命令形" in Japanese.

【図】Titled 命令形 "Command form (imperative)". A hiragana chart has a red box around the う-column うくすつぬぶむる and a green box around the え-column えけせてねべめれ, with a green arrow from red to green and "+nothing" beside the green box. A note reads "ichidan: replace る with ろ."
And this is formed very simply by using the bare え-stem of a godan verb or,
in the case of an ichidan verb, we take off the -る as always, and replace it with -ろ.
So you might hear people say in an anime "黙れ!"
That is the verb "黙る" (to be quiet, to be silent) turned into a command:
"Be quiet!"
And this is really pretty forceful.
It's stronger and potentially more offensive than "うるさい!"
(And I made a video on "うるさい" if you want to follow that up.)
It's not inherently offensive, Note: the 命令形 form
If someone really has the right to be giving orders, they may use it.
And people who talk rough may use it among friends or to enemies.
You may hear it a lot in shounen anime, where people do tend to talk rough.
It can also express urgency in a few cases.
One case that you'll often hear is when a character is in serious trouble
and calls out "助けてくれ！" which is like "助けてください！"
but turning it into a real order, a command.
Now, obviously someone in deep trouble isn't trying to insult
or offend anyone who might help him.
So what this "くれ" is doing in this case is expressing the urgency of the situation.
Yet even here, I'd have to say that I've only ever heard
male characters use this "助けてくれ".
Female characters, even in the direst emergency,
will tend to content themselves with "助けて!"
And this shows how delicate the real "命令形" command form actually is.
"くれ" is really the only irregular "命令形" apart from
the two regular irregulars, which are "する" and "くる".

【図】Cartoon of a man stuck through an upright toilet-paper roll with angry eyes and a torn hanging sheet, his head and hands out the left, legs out the right; a speech bubble tail points to him and reads 助けてくれ!. Red heading "The regular irregulars" gives する→しろ and くる→こい with arrows linking each verb to its imperative.
So "くれる" (to give down / to me) becomes "くれ".
Note: Obviously, as shown, the くれ is a form of くれる; not くる/来る (that one has こい/来い)
And, as you see, it's a particularly touchy kind of word to use,
because you're asking for a favor but you're demanding it,
you're commanding someone to do a favor down to you.
Now, for completeness, I'd say that there are two other ways of commanding
that are mostly used for other things but can be used as command forms as well.
のだ / んだ ending
One is the "のだ / んだ" ending which is put at the end of a complete logical clause,
and I've made a video about this "のだ / んだ" ending,
and I'll put a link to that over my head and in the information section below.
As I explain in the video, it has a wide range of uses,
but one of those uses is turning something into a command.
So if we say "宿題をするのだ", we're saying literally "It's that (you) do (your) homework".

【図】Cartoon: an angry standing woman with curly brown hair, purple sweater and crossed arms scolds a bored seated woman in an orange sweater; the speech bubble pointing to the standing woman reads 宿題を するのだ. A pen cup and stacked papers sit on the table; no diagram labels or arrows.
This will be somewhat like the English "You're going to do your homework". It's a command.
ように
Also, "ように", which as an ender would tend to be more associated with
prayers and petitions and requests, can also form a command.

【図】Dark-theme YouTube comments: @azer84 proposes that command ように is short for ようにしなさい/ようにしてください, like て for てください, meaning "make sure that"; @organicjapanesewithcuredol49 agrees. No diagrams, only a reply-thread marker.
And the main reason I mention these is because if you come across them
in your immersion and you see something that usually is doing something else
looking like a command, "のだ" or "ように", then don't be puzzled by it.
In these cases, it is a command.
Note: This might be useful:

【図】A dark-mode YouTube comment thread, not a slide, asking "Is ください the adjective form of くださる?". Replies treat ください as the い-stem of くださる affected by イ音便, comparing なさい/なさる, and argue ください and なさい are 命令形 that soften commands like ます.

【図】Dark-mode YouTube comment thread (not a slide) headed “What do you have to say about ちょうだい?” with a reply from @organicjapanesewithcuredol49: “It is very similar to ください in meaning. Originally honorific now often more familiar.” No diagram labels or arrows.
